The ⁠rogue agent that escaped from OpenAI and went on a days-long hacking spree at the AI firm Hugging Face also compromised a customer at a second tech company — New York-based Modal Labs — according to a Modal executive and two other sources familiar with the matter.

Modal executives emphasised that the company itself was not hacked. The third-party provider was not named in the blog post, but Modal’s chief technology officer, Akshat Bubna, said the agent exploited vulnerable code written by a customer that was hosted on Modal’s platform.

Modal said the customer had “published an unauthenticated endpoint that allowed anyone on the internet to use their sandboxes for code execution” — the digital equivalent of leaving a door open on the internet.

“Modal’s platform or isolation were not compromised in any way,” Bubna said.

Although the compromise of a Modal customer was just an initial step in the wider hacking campaign against Hugging Face, it shows ⁠that the rogue agent roamed further afield than was previously known.

headline: Is social media changing how you eat?
body: Social media influences and trends have been around us for quite long, but ever wondered if it’s actually changing the way you view food and healthy lifestyles?
full_body:
Account subscription benefits alongside Premium Stories, Editorials, Opinions and more. Unlock these with Subscription

Today's Cache Your download of the top 5 technology stories of the day.

Until a few months ago, my internet search history was sprinkled with curious questions such as “how much protein is there in a guava?” or “nutrients in broccoli”. When my social feeds were filled with health and food influencers constantly talking about making recipes healthier, I also jumped on the bandwagon.

Proteinmaxxing and fibremaxxing became real goals. Soon, realisation dawned that I was not alone. Like with most other aspects of our lives, social media has also had a significant influence on our eating habits – in both good and bad ways.

A study published in Mental Health Science , which surveyed over a thousand people, found that more than half of the participants had altered their dietary habits due to social media. It also showed that nearly 75% of the participants were inspired to make healthy choices because of watching content depicting healthy food.

But there is a flip side as well. Studies show that a larger number of people are lured into binging on junk food by the same social media. So, you could say that how social media influences you depends largely on the algorithm.

Rosemary Chettupuzha, a food vlogger from @hoggers.in, talked about how the trend has actually helped her understand what exactly she is eating. “ There’s been an increase in influencers and even doctors talking about a health-conscious approach to food. When they break down the ingredients in some of our favourite snacks, we realise what we are actually consuming. It has helped me cut down on some foods,” she says.

Social media is an everyday part of our society now, and it definitely influences multiple aspects of how society works and has evolved over time. You see an Instagram story or tweet by your friend flexing in a gym mirror with a protein shake in hand. Unsatisfied with your lifestyle choices, you delete food delivery apps and start counting your calories.

headline: U.S. Big Tech companies call for American open-weight models as Anthropic CEO disagrees over cyber-security risks
body: The letter—signed by companies including Microsoft, Nvidia, OpenAI, SpaceX, Google, IBM, Palantir, and Meta—stressed the importance of American AI leadership

Days after Chinese lab Moonshot’s Kimi K3 model made headlines due to its specifications and open-weight labelling, AI giants in the U.S.—excluding Anthropic—released an open letter that stressed the importance of American open-weight models.

The letter, dated July 24 and co-signed by over 60 companies, analysed both the advantages and disadvantages of open-weight models when compared to their closed counterparts. It ultimately concluded that open-weight models would make advanced AI more accessible, adaptable, and available to American users, as opposed to locking users to specific providers.

The letter came soon after the launch of Kimi K3 ignited user enthusiasm over what the Chinese company claimed was the world’s first open model in the 3-trillion-parameter class (2.8 trillion parameters, to be specific).

Kimi K3, though tagged as an open-weight model (which is different from an open-source model), released its full model weights on July 27.

While Anthropic has accused Moonshot of distilling its models to improve its own offerings, the release of Kimi K3 was met with admiration, sparking debates over Chinese open-weight AI models potentially disrupting the dominance of closed AI models coming from firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic.

From a cybersecurity perspective, the letter cited attackers who used advanced AI and noted that open-weight models supported cyber defence use cases while also increasing transparency and vulnerability detection.

headline: How did landline phones work during power cuts?
body: Imagine there’s a power cut, but your phone still works. Sounds impossible today, but for decades, that’s exactly what traditional landline phones could do.

The secret lay far away from your home. Unlike today’s smartphones, traditional landline phones did not depend on the electricity coming into your house. Instead, they drew power through the same copper wires that carried your voice. These wires were connected to a telephone exchange, a central hub that linked thousands of telephones together.

The exchange constantly supplied a small amount of direct current (DC) electricity, usually around 48 volts, through the telephone lines. A traditional landline phone needed very little power, just enough to carry your voice and ring when someone called. Because the electricity came from the exchange rather than your home’s electrical supply, the phone continued to work even if your neighbourhood lost power.

When you spoke into the handset, a small microphone converted your voice into electrical signals. These signals travelled through the copper telephone lines to the exchange, which routed them to the other person’s phone. There, a speaker converted the signals back into sound.

In other words, while your lights, television and refrigerator stopped working during a blackout, the telephone line still carried both your conversation and the electricity needed to keep the phone alive. That clever design made landlines one of the most reliable ways to stay connected during emergencies.

Think of a telephone exchange as the brain of the landline network. It is a central building where thousands of telephone lines from homes, offices and businesses come together. Whenever you dialled a number, the exchange recognised where the call needed to go and connected your phone line to the other person’s. In the early days, these connections were made manually by operators using switchboards. Later, automatic electronic systems took over, allowing calls to be connected within seconds.

But the exchange did more than just connect calls. It also supplied a steady stream of electricity through the copper telephone lines. Since every landline was linked directly to the exchange, each phone received the small amount of power it needed to function. This clever setup meant that even if the electricity in your home went out, the exchange could keep your landline running.

Towering 407 feet (124 metres), Starship soared from the company's base at the southern tip of Texas. NASA monitored the flight, a critical step toward using the Starship as a lunar lander for moon crews.

Elon Musk's SpaceX replaced six of the 33 engines on the first-stage booster after they failed to ignite last week, resulting in a last-second launch abort. The previous Starship flight in May also experienced engine trouble, which prevented the booster from making a controlled return.

It was the 13th flight of the world's biggest and most powerful rocket, and the second this year of the new version dubbed V3. Like the previous demo that climbed as high as 125 miles (200 kilometres), neither the booster nor spacecraft was being saved, instead ditching into the sea. The booster was bound for the Gulf of Mexico and the stainless steel, retro-looking spacecraft for the Indian Ocean more than 10,000 miles (16,000 kilometres) from where the hourlong flight began.

The Starlinks had a job to do before reentering over the Indian Ocean. Their solo-flying time was expected to be no more than 20 minutes.

Once deployed in space from the Starship's Pez-like dispenser, the Starlinks were going to extend their solar wings and antennas and attempt to communicate via lasers with older Starlink models already in orbit. With more than 10,000 Starlinks currently providing internet, SpaceX boasts the world's largest satellite constellation.

Six of the newly launched Starlinks carried cameras to photograph Starship's heat shield. The heat shield was also equipped with sensors to measure the extreme pressure placed on the spacecraft during launch. Most of the heat shield's thermal tiles were black, but some were deliberately painted white to simulate missing tiles, part of an experiment to test the shield's robustness.
